"It's clear that somebody just got mad about something and decided to break the window," said Richard Tousignant, owner of the mattress palace for 26 years. Despite its name, the Palais also stocks furniture and stocks it wherever there's floor space, so if you happen iO be walking down one of the store's two aisles and someone's coming the other way, one of you had better be ready to either shinny up the side of a mclaminc dres&r or test the comfort of the queen-size Orthop5dique. "This isn't the kind of place where you'd want to . rob something," said Tousignant, speaking with the, kind of composure that comes from knowing a hitherto unblemished insurance record means the $2,500 claim for the windows will not be a problem. "What's to take? A chest of drawers? And even if you sell it, what do you get? Twenty dollars?" Like everyone else on the street who was busy picking up the pieces yesterday, Tousignant knows that many if not all of those involved in Sunday's riot were black. And like anyone else who has lived his entire life in this neighborhood ("I came into the world over on Jean Talon"), a neighborhood composed of people whom white demographers like to label "ethnic," Tousignant couldn't care less. Not even an argument "Couple of years ago the black community here had a huge festival, one end of the street to the other," he leaned forward across the work orders that covered his desk at the back of the store. "No problems. Nothing. Not even an argument. "But," he said, leaning back again, "the past four , or five years there have been bands of young people; wandering the street. A lot of them black. But even then nothing ever happened." Tousignant figures that things just snowballed on Sunday night, that alcohol, an argument, a gun and all that glass just added up to two guys standing " outside his store yesterday, getting ready to heft in a new display window. Not everybody saw it that way, however. Up in Quebec City, where the snow on Mont Stc. text: FES KASBAT This very pretty Moroccan restaurant has low sofas and tables in semi-private "booths" along its sides and standard tables in the middle. It offers a much wider range of Moroccan cuisine than its simpler cousins, the ubiquitous couscous houses. Try any of the excellent briks or chef's fingers for starters. The place does feature a wide range of couscous dishes, of course, well made but timidly seasoned. A better bet are its tajines (stews cooked in earthenware casseroles), although the one sampled chicken with olives and rice was barely saved from terminal blandness by the wonderful Moroccan pickled lemon slices. A small dash of fiery harissa can correct this timidity in a hurry, but a word in the ear of the waitress when ordering might be more productive.
